title: Chapter 6 – The Skeletal System: Bone Tissue
notes: Skeletal system functions: support, protection, movement, mineral homeostasis, blood cell production, triglyceride storage.
Long bone anatomy: diaphysis, epiphyses, metaphyses, articular cartilage, periosteum, medullary cavity, endosteum.
Bone ECM: ~15% water, 30% collagen, 55% mineral salts (hydroxyapatite).
Cells: osteoprogenitors → osteoblasts (build) → osteocytes (maintain); osteoclasts resorb.
Compact bone: osteons; Spongy bone: trabeculae with red marrow.
Blood/nerve supply through nutrient foramina, periosteal vessels, metaphyseal/epiphyseal vessels.
Ossification: intramembranous (flat bones) vs endochondral (most bones).
Longitudinal growth at epiphyseal plates; appositional growth thickens bones.
Bone remodeling couples osteoclast resorption with osteoblast deposition.
Hormones: GH/IGFs, thyroid hormones, sex hormones; vitamins A/C/D/K/B12; minerals Ca2+, P, Mg, etc.
Fracture repair: reactive (hematoma), reparative (fibrocartilaginous then bony callus), remodeling.
Calcium homeostasis: PTH ↑ blood Ca2+; calcitriol ↑ intestinal absorption; calcitonin (thyroid) can ↓ blood Ca2+.
Exercise increases bone density via mechanical stress; disuse leads to loss.
Aging shifts toward resorption; osteoporosis risk increases (esp. post‑menopausal).
Compact bone resists bending; spongy bone reduces weight and supports marrow.
Endochondral ossification replaces cartilage template; primary/secondary ossification centers.
Periosteum contains osteogenic cells; essential for growth and repair.
Hydroxyapatite crystals provide hardness; collagen provides tensile strength.
Epiphyseal plate zones: resting, proliferating, hypertrophic, calcified cartilage.
High PTH elevates osteoclast activity; negative feedback controls blood Ca2+.
Open vs closed fractures, stress fractures; proper alignment essential for healing.
Vitamin D deficiency: rickets (children) / osteomalacia (adults).
Wolff’s law: bone adapts to loads placed upon it.
